entries.7bf35c4d5d43db7601d07a3b618e4fb6d6be894d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.6-1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen3924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3925" type="x-p"/> When they came, sc., to the sacrificial meal, which was no doubt held in Jesse’s house, after the sacrifice had been presented upon an altar, and when Samuel saw the eldest son Eliab, who was tall and handsome according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:7</reference>, “<hi type="italic">he thought</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. he said, sc., in his heart), <hi type="italic">Surely His anointed is before Jehovah</hi>,” i.e., surely the man is now standing before Jehovah whom He hath chosen to be His anointed. But Jehovah said to him in the spirit, “<hi type="italic">Look not at his form and the height of his stature, for I have rejected him: for not as man seeth</hi> (sc., do I see); <hi type="italic">for man looketh at the eyes, and Jehovah looketh at the heart</hi>.” The eyes, as contrasted with the heart, are figuratively employed to denote the outward form.
entries.a1e48578078d84e9e105fe84f9c7fd7c7d390b79: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.8-1Sam.16.10">1Sa 16:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen3925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3926" type="x-p"/> When Jesse thereupon brought up his other sons, one after another, before Samuel, the prophet said in the case of each, “<hi type="italic">This also Jehovah hath not chosen</hi>.” As Samuel must be the subject to the verb ויּאמר in <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.8-1Sam.16.10">1Sa 16:8-10</reference>, we may assume that he had communicated the object of his coming to Jesse.
entries.66c256fe7396e4bdaac9d732c89955f2d7f06c19: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.11">1Sa 16:11</reference> <div eID="gen3926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3927" type="x-p"/> After the seventh had been presented, and the Lord had not pointed nay one of them out as the chosen one, “<hi type="italic">Samuel said to Jesse, Are these all the boys?</hi>” When Jesse replied that there was still <hi type="italic">the smallest</hi>, i.e., the youngest, left, and he was keeping the sheep, he directed him to fetch him; “<hi type="italic">for</hi>,” said he, “<hi type="italic">we will not sit down till he has come hither</hi>,” סבב, to surround, sc., the table, upon which the meal was arranged. This is implied in the context.
entries.5279e59955b68909c1c22711cec64552bee0d3a1: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.12-1Sam.16.13">1Sa 16:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen3927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3928" type="x-p"/> When David arrived, - and he was <hi type="italic">ruddy</hi>, also <hi type="italic">of beautiful eyes and good looks</hi> (אדמוני, used to denote the reddish colour of the hair, which was regarded as a mark of beauty in southern lands, where the hair is generally black. עם is an adverb here = therewith), and therefore, so far as his looks and figure were concerned, well fitted, notwithstanding his youth, for the office to which the Lord had chosen him, since corporeal beauty was one of the outward distinctions of a king, - the Lord pointed him out to the prophet as the chosen one; whereupon he anointed him in the midst of his brethren. Along with the anointing the Spirit of Jehovah came upon David from that day forward. But Samuel returned to Ramah when the sacrificial meal was over. There is nothing recorded concerning any words of Samuel to David at the time of the anointing and in explanation of its meaning, as in the case of Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">1Sa 10:1</reference>). In all probability Samuel said nothing at the time, since, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.2">1Sa 16:2</reference>, he had good reason for keeping the matter secret, not only on his own account, but still more for David’s sake; so that even the brethren of David who were present knew nothing about the meaning and object of the anointing, but may have imagined that Samuel merely intended to consecrate David as a pupil of the prophets. At the same time, we can hardly suppose that Samuel left Jesse, and even David, in uncertainty as to the object of his mission, and of the anointing which he had performed. He may have communicated all this to both of them, without letting the other sons know. It by no means follows, that because David remained with his father and kept the sheep as before, therefore his calling to be king must have been unknown to him; but only that in the anointing which he had received he did not discern either the necessity or obligation to appear openly as the anointed of the Lord, and that after receiving the Spirit of the Lord in consequence of the anointing, he left the further development of the matter to the Lord in childlike submission, assured that He would prepare and show him the way to the throne in His own good time. <div eID="gen3928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3929" type="x-p"/> David’s Introduction to the Court of Saul. - 1Sa 16:14. With the rejection of Saul on the part of God, the Spirit of Jehovah had departed from him, and an evil spirit from Jehovah had come upon him, who filled him with fear and anguish. The “<hi type="italic">evil spirit from Jehovah</hi>” which came into Saul in the place of the Spirit of Jehovah, was not merely an inward feeling of depression at the rejection announced to him, which grew into melancholy, and occasionally broke out in passing fits of insanity, but a higher evil power, which took possession of him, and not only deprived him of his peace of mind, but stirred up the feelings, ideas, imagination, and thoughts of his soul to such an extent that at times it drove him even into madness. This demon is called “<hi type="italic">an evil spirit</hi> (coming) <hi type="italic">from Jehovah</hi>,” because Jehovah had sent it as a punishment, or “<hi type="italic">an evil spirit of God</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.15">1Sa 16:15</reference>), or briefly “<hi type="italic">a spirit of God</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>), or “<hi type="italic">the evil spirit</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.23">1Sa 16:23</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference>), as being a supernatural, spiritual, evil power; but never “the Spirit of Jehovah,” because this is the Spirit proceeding from the holy God, which works upon men as the spirit of strength, wisdom, and knowledge, and generates and fosters the spiritual or divine life. The expression רעה יהוה רוּח   (<reference osisRef="1Sam.19.9">1Sa 19:9</reference>) is an abbreviated form for יהוה מאת רעה רוּח, and is to be interpreted according.
entries.5c262a69977bd15d6e5a6a4f448b6ef9d665ff7d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.15-1Sam.16.16">1Sa 16:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen3929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3930" type="x-p"/> When Saul’s attendants, i.e., his officers at court, perceived the mental ailment of the king, they advised him to let the evil spirit which troubled him be charmed away by instrumental music. “<hi type="italic">Let our lord speak</hi> (command); <hi type="italic">thy servants are before thee</hi> (i.e., ready to serve thee): <hi type="italic">they will seek a man skilled in playing upon the harp; so will it be well with thee when an evil spirit of God comes upon thee, and he</hi> (the man referred to) <hi type="italic">plays with his hands</hi>.” The powerful influence exerted by music upon the state of the mind was well known even in the earliest times; so that the wise men of ancient Greece recommended music to soothe the passions, to heal mental diseases, and even to check tumults among the people. From the many examples collected by <hi type="italic">Grotius</hi>, Clericus, and more especially Bochart in the <hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. P. i. l. 2, c. 44, we will merely cite the words of Censorinus (<hi type="italic">de die natali</hi>, c. 12): “<hi type="italic">Pythagoras ut animum sua semper divinitate imbueret, priusquam se somno daret et cum esset expergitus, cithara ut ferunt cantare consueverat, et Asclepiades medicus phreneticorum mentes morbo turbatas saepe per symphoniam suae naturae reddidit.</hi>”
entries.b77847b550ee90d96b1aa5b9139e12c73ffc0ff1: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.17-1Sam.16.18">1Sa 16:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen3930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3931" type="x-p"/> When Saul commanded them to seek out a good player upon a stringed instrument in accordance with this advice, one of the youths (נערים, a lower class of court servants) said, “<hi type="italic">I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, skilled in laying, and a brave man, and a man of war, eloquent, and a handsome man, and Jehovah is with him</hi>.” The description of David is “<hi type="italic">a mighty man</hi>” and “<hi type="italic">a man of war</hi>” does not presuppose that David had already fought bravely in war, but may be perfectly explained from what David himself afterwards affirmed respecting his conflicts with lions and bears (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.35">1Sa 17:34-35</reference>). The courage and strength which he had then displayed furnished sufficient proofs of heroism for any one to discern in him the future warrior.
entries.3ecfff1b6eb55e860d215a14a1cee3417b3e8606: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.19-1Sam.16.20">1Sa 16:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen3931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3932" type="x-p"/> Saul thereupon sent to ask Jesse for his son David; and Jesse sent him with a present of an ass’s burden of bread, a bottle of wine, and a buck-kid. Instead of the singular expression לחם חמור, an ass with bread, i.e., laden with bread, the lxx read לחם חמר, and rendered it γόμορ ἄρτων; but this is certainly wrong, as they were not accustomed to measure bread in bushels. These presents show how simple were the customs of Israel and in the court of Saul at that time.
entries.8d3a7fa0a834675dd815416912565e3d99f41c1e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.21-1Sam.16.23">1Sa 16:21-23</reference> <div eID="gen3932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3933" type="x-p"/> When David came to Saul and stood before him, i.e., served him by playing upon his harp, Saul took a great liking to him, and nominated him his armour-bearer, i.e., his adjutant, as a proof of his satisfaction with him, and sent to Jesse to say, “<hi type="italic">Let David stand before me</hi>,” i.e., remain in my service, “<hi type="italic">for he has found favour in my sight</hi>.” The historian then adds (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.23">1Sa 16:23</reference>): “<hi type="italic">When the</hi> (evil) <hi type="italic">spirit of God came to Saul</hi> (אל, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.9">1Sa 19:9</reference>, is really equivalent to על), <hi type="italic">and David took the harp and played, there came refreshing to Saul, and he became well, and the evil spirit departed from him</hi>.” Thus David came to Saul’s court, and that as his benefactor, without Saul having any suspicion of David’s divine election to be king of Israel. This guidance on the part of God was a school of preparation to David for his future calling. In the first place, he was thereby lifted out of his quiet and homely calling in the country into the higher sphere of court-life; and thus an opportunity was afforded him not only for intercourse with men of high rank, and to become acquainted with the affairs of the kingdom, but also to display those superior gifts of his intellect and heart with which God had endowed him, and thereby to gain the love and confidence of the people. But at the same time he was also brought into a severe school of affliction, in which his inner man was to be trained by conflicts from without and within, so that he might become a man after God’s heart, who should be well fitted to found the true monarchy in Israel. A war between the Philistines and the Israelites furnished David with the opportunity of displaying before Saul and all Israel, and greatly to the terror of the enemies of his people, that heroic power which was firmly based upon his bold and pious trust in the omnipotence of the faithful covenant God (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.1-1Sam.17.3">1Sa 17:1-3</reference>). A powerful giant, named Goliath, came forward from the ranks of the Philistines, and scornfully challenged the Israelites to produce a man who would decide the war by a single combat with him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.4-1Sam.17.11">1Sa 17:4-11</reference>). David, who had returned home for a time from the court of Saul, and had just been sent into the camp by his father with provisions for his elder brothers who were serving in the army, as soon as he heard the challenge and the scornful words of the Philistine, offered to fight with him (vv. 15-37), and killed the giant with a stone from a sling; whereupon the Philistines took to flight, and were pursued by the Israelites to Gath and Ekron (vv. 38-54).  <chapter eID="1Sam.16"/> <div eID="gen3933" type="x-p"/>
